When fitting a regression model, the intercept is probably not the coefficient
that you spend the most time thinking about. It represents the baseline
response, is usually left unpenalized, and rarely gets much attention in
discussions of optimization algorithms. But it turns out that the way you update
this one coefficient can have a substantial effect on how quickly the entire
model fits.

Me and Frederik Fabricius-Bjerre study this in a new paper of ours: *How to
Train Your Intercept: A Comparison of Intercept Update Strategies in Coordinate
Descent*\ [@larsson2026c], we study this choice for regularized generalized
linear models. The [code and manuscript
source](https://github.com/jolars/intercepts) are available on GitHub. Our main
finding is that, when the response is imbalanced, a conservative (but common)
intercept update can slow down the whole solver. A single Newton step, with a
safeguard against overshooting, largely removes this slowdown in our
experiments.

To make this concrete, consider @fig-convergence. We fit the same regularized
logistic regression model to the w1a dataset\ [@platt1998] with three strategies
for updating the intercept. Everything else in our solver stays the same. The
Newton and exact strategies reach a relative suboptimality below $10^{-8}$ after
roughly 45 passes over the coordinates. The gradient strategy needs more than
*seven* times as many passes.

![Convergence on w1a under three intercept-update strategies. Lower values mean
that the objective is closer to its optimum.](images/convergence.svg){#fig-convergence width="600px" fig-alt="Relative suboptimality bound versus elapsed time on w1a. Newton and exact intercept updates converge much sooner than the conservative gradient update."}

So, the treatment of the intercept *can* make a large difference, but this is
nowhere examined in the literature. My interest in this topic grew from noticing
that implementation of optimization algorithms often take different approaches
to updating the intercept even though they largely agree on the right approach
to update every other coefficient. And these papers neither explain nor justify
their choice.

This lead me to pose this problem as a project for a project course in
statistics at my department. One of the students who picked and worked on that
project was Frederik. Afterwards, we continued to work on this topic and have
now finally wrapped up the work and submitted it to a journal.

## The intercept in logistic regression

A logistic regression model describes the probability of a positive response as
$$
  p_i = \Pr(Y_i = 1 \mid x_i) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[-(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta)]},
$$
where $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $\beta$ contains the feature coefficients.
If all the feature coefficients are zero, the intercept alone determines the
predicted probability. For example, a probability of $0.01$ corresponds to an
intercept of approximately $-4.6$.

We fit the model by minimizing the logistic loss plus a penalty on $\beta$, such
as the lasso penalty\ [@tibshirani1996]. The intercept is not penalized. A
common way to solve this problem is *coordinate descent*, which repeatedly
updates one coefficient at a time while holding the others fixed.^[I have
previously worked on coordinate descent for SLOPE\ [@larsson2023], which is what
has lead me to look into this issue. If you are not familiar with coordinate but
want to learn more, @wright2015 provides an accessible overview.] We call a
sweep over the coefficient coordinates a *pass*. In coordinate descent the
intercept is one of the coordinates, but it has special properties: its update
is smooth because it has no penalty, and it remains part of every pass.

## Three ways to update the intercept

We compare three strategies, each applied once per pass over the feature
coefficients:

The gradient strategy
:   Take one step using a global, worst-case bound on the curvature of the loss.

The Newton strategy

:   Take one step using the curvature at the current fit.

The exact strategy
:   Minimize the loss over the intercept while holding the feature coefficients
    fixed.^[In the experiments, we solve this subproblem numerically to a tight
    tolerance.]

@fig-trajectories illustrates these choices for a small logistic regression
problem with one feature. The curves follow the intercept and feature
coefficient as the solver approaches the solution. The gradient strategy takes
many small steps, whereas the Newton and exact strategies arrive in only a few.

![Intercept and coefficient trajectories on a one-feature logistic regression
problem. The gray contours show level sets of the objective.](images/trajectories.svg){#fig-trajectories width="600px" fig-alt="Objective contours with three optimization paths. The gradient path approaches the solution gradually, while the Newton and exact paths reach it in a few steps."}

## Why imbalance matters

For logistic regression, the curvature of the averaged loss in the intercept
direction is
$$
  H_{00} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1 - p_i).
$$
Since $p_i(1 - p_i)$ is at most $1/4$, we can use $L_0 = 1/4$ as a global
curvature bound. If $g_0$ denotes the derivative of the loss with respect to the
intercept, the gradient and full Newton updates are, respectively,
$$
  \beta_0 \leftarrow \beta_0 - \frac{g_0}{L_0}, \qquad \beta_0
          \leftarrow \beta_0 - \frac{g_0}{H_{00}}.
$$

The gradient step is a reasonable choice when the current curvature is close to
its upper bound. But when fitted probabilities approach zero or one,
$p_i(1 - p_i)$ becomes small, and the two step sizes can differ greatly. In an
intercept-only model with a fitted probability of $0.01$, the curvature is
$0.0099$. The full Newton step is then about 25 times as large as the gradient
step.^[This compares step sizes at the same iterate and does not imply a 25-fold
improvement in performance.]

A small intercept step would matter less if the intercept could be optimized
independently of the other coefficients. But they are typically
coupled---updating a feature coefficient can move the intercept's conditional
optimum. If the next intercept update leaves it far from that optimum, the
remaining error also affects the gradients used to update the feature
coefficients. This gives two parts of the explanation: low curvature makes the
conservative intercept update small, and coupling allows the resulting intercept
error to slow progress in the rest of the model. Response imbalance makes this
mechanism important in our experiments, but imbalance alone does not determine
how much slower a particular fit will be.

## Doesn't centering solve this?

If you are familiar with linear regression, you might wonder why we cannot just
center the features and separate the intercept from the slopes.

For squared loss, that works. The cross-curvature between the intercept and
coefficient $j$ is proportional to the mean of feature $j$. Centering makes that
mean zero, so the intercept decouples from the feature coefficients.

For logistic regression, the corresponding quantity is instead
$$
  H_{0j} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1 - p_i)x_{ij}.
$$
This is a weighted feature mean. Ordinary centering makes the unweighted mean
zero, but generally leaves this weighted mean nonzero. Moreover, the weights
change as we fit the model. Standardizing the features therefore does not
necessarily remove the interaction between the intercept and the slopes.

In our [earlier work on normalization](../2025-01-21-normreg/index.qmd), we
focused on how feature scaling changes regularization\ [@larsson2025]. Centering
was simpler: with an unpenalized intercept, we could center the features without
changing the fitted model. That remains true for logistic regression, but the
computational benefit does not carry over. Ordinary centering no longer
separates the intercept from the slopes.

## How much work should we spend on the intercept?

If a lagging intercept causes trouble, an obvious response is to optimize it
fully after every pass. But our experiments suggest that this is usually wasted
work. One safeguarded Newton step typically follows nearly the same outer
trajectory as exact intercept minimization, while requiring fewer inner steps.
The reason is that the next sweep over the feature coefficients moves the
intercept's conditional optimum again. Solving the intercept subproblem very
accurately before that sweep can therefore spend effort on accuracy that will
soon be lost.

The safeguard matters too. Newton uses a local quadratic approximation, and its
full step can overshoot when that approximation is poor. We observe this in a
Poisson cold-start example. A backtracking line search makes the update useful
without relying on the full step always being safe.

## What happens in existing solvers?

We also study six production solvers. An important distinction is whether a
solver applies coordinate descent directly to the original GLM loss or first
builds a quadratic approximation and solves that approximation by coordinate
descent. Within a frozen local quadratic, the intercept curvature is already
available, and optimizing the intercept is straightforward. A quadratic based on
a worst-case curvature bound can retain the same conservatism as the direct
gradient strategy.

### skglm

One particularly instructive example comes from
(skglm)[https://contrib.scikit-learn.org/skglm/]. Its historical intercept
update in version 0.5 was even more conservative than our gradient baseline: its
step was sixteen times smaller. We submitted a patch replacing that update with
a Newton step and compared the commits immediately before and after the fix on
the same family of problems. As you can see, the differences in @fig-skglm are
substantial.

![Iteration-count comparison between the historical and Newton intercept
updates in skglm. Larger values indicate a greater reduction in iterations
after the patch.](images/skglm-comparison.svg){#fig-skglm width="500px" fig-alt="Heatmap of the base-10 logarithm of pre-fix to post-fix mean iteration counts in skglm, across response imbalance and relative regularization strength. The differences are largest under extreme imbalance and weak regularization."}

### Solvers using iteratively reweighted least squares

Solvers such as glmnet\ [@friedman2010] use iteratively reweighted least squares
(IRLS) to build a local quadratic approximation of the loss. In these cases, the
intercept problem is already a simple weighted least squares problem, and the
different strategies collapse to the same update. So none of these solvers
suffer from the slow convergence that we observe in our experiments. I have
become more and more convinced that IRLS is the better approach for generalized
linear models. Anecdotally, I have found that it often avoids some convergence
traps that direct coordinate descent can fall into.

## Recommendations

Most of the time our results favor one safeguarded Newton intercept update per
pass. This is both simple and effective. It avoids the convergence trap that the
gradient strategy leads to and avoids wasting work on a more complex
implementation that adds no benefit in all but a few edge cases.

Our theoretical explanation is local and we do not prove a general global
convergence rate for coordinate descent with Newton intercept updates.
Nevertheless, our analysis and experiments point to the same practical lesson:
keeping the intercept in step with the feature coefficients can make a large
difference, and doing so often requires only one well-chosen update per pass.
